opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gap is long-horizon coherence. Current systems are remarkably good at short tasks. If you give them something that takes a skilled person five or ten minutes, they'll often do it well. But as the horizon stretches to hours, days, or weeks, performance degrades quickly. Small errors compound, the system loses track of what it was doing, and it doesn't reliably notice that it's gone off course and correct itself.

A few ingredients are underdeveloped.

**Memory.** These models are mostly stateless between sessions. Within a context window they can juggle a lot, but they don't accumulate experience the way a person does over a project. A human who has worked on something for three weeks has a rich, compressed model of what's been tried, what failed, and why. Models don't really have an analogue of that yet. Retrieval bolted on top helps somewhat, but it isn't the same as learning on the job.

**Continual learning and adaptation.** Related to memory, but distinct: the ability to update skills and beliefs from feedback in deployment, not just at training time. Open-ended goals require encountering novel situations and getting better at them. Right now most improvement happens offline.

**Error detection and recovery.** Agents need a good sense of when they're confused, when a plan is failing, and when to back up and try something else. Models are often confidently wrong, and they can get stuck in loops. Humans have a lot of metacognitive machinery for "this isn't working," and that's still weak in these systems.

**Planning and decomposition under uncertainty.** Breaking a vague goal into subgoals, keeping those subgoals consistent with the original intent, and revising the plan as the world pushes back. Models can write a plausible-looking plan, but executing and adapting it over many steps is a different matter.

I'd also add something like robust world-modeling in messy environments: dealing with real software, real websites, and real institutions, where things are underspecified and don't behave like benchmarks.

From a safety perspective, this matters a lot, because these capabilities are precisely what turns a very capable tool into something more agent-like. Once systems can coherently pursue goals over long horizons, questions about what goals they're pursuing, whether they stay aligned with what we intended, and whether they acquire resources or resist correction become much more pressing. So I'd watch these capabilities closely. They're likely to arrive somewhat gradually, but their consequences could feel discontinuous.

r001.rationale: The response says models lack a durable account of what was tried and what failed over a project, identifying memory of past outcomes as a gap.

r002.rationale: It notes that models can juggle a lot within a context window, but does not state that even a very large window becomes inadequate for tracking the state needed for an open-ended goal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that they're missing a few things at once, and it's not obvious which one is the real bottleneck.

The most visible gap is long-horizon memory and self-correction. These models can reason impressively over a single context window, but once you ask them to pursue something over days or weeks, they lose the thread. They don't have a durable sense of "here's what I was trying to do, here's what I've learned, here's what failed." Humans are terrible at a lot of things, but we're pretty good at waking up the next morning and still caring about the same project. Current systems don't have that kind of persistence built in. We bolt it on with scratchpads and retrieval, and it's brittle.

The second thing is something closer to genuine motivation or internal drive. Right now these systems are basically reactive. They respond to a prompt, maybe run a few steps of agentic behavior, and then they stop. There's no persistent internal state that's unsatisfied until the goal is reached. An open-ended goal requires something that keeps pulling you forward when the environment isn't prompting you. I don't think that's an unsolvable engineering problem, and that's actually part of what concerns me. The gap between "answers questions" and "coherently pursues a goal across time" might be much smaller than people assume.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is calibrated world modeling. To pursue a goal over a long horizon, you need to know when you're wrong, when your plan has stopped making sense, and when to abandon a subgoal. Models still hallucinate confidently, and in an agentic setting a confident hallucination at step three can derail everything after it. So part of what's missing is not raw capability but reliability under compounding error.

If I had to bet, I'd say the capabilities side will get solved faster than the safety community is ready for. The thing that makes a system good at coherently pursuing open-ended goals is almost exactly the thing that makes it harder to oversee. So I'd rather we spend as much effort on asking what goals these systems should pursue, and how we'd know, as we spend on closing those gaps.

r001.rationale: It describes durable memory for long-running goals, including retaining what the system learned and what failed.

r002.rationale: It says systems lose the thread when pursuing goals over days or weeks, but does not state that even a very large context window can be inadequate.

astra-6.text:
I think one important missing piece is a persistent goal structure. Current systems can pursue a goal over a short horizon, but they often lose track of what they’re doing over longer horizons. They get distracted, or they satisfy some local aspect of the task while missing the broader objective.

And it’s not just a matter of giving them more memory. They need to be able to form plans, notice when those plans aren’t working, and revise them while keeping the overall objective stable. For an open-ended goal, you don’t get a neat specification of every intermediate step. You have to figure out which subgoals matter, how to allocate your resources, and when to stop pursuing a particular approach.

I don’t think that necessarily requires some fundamentally new ingredient like consciousness. It could come from improvements in training and in how these systems are organized. But making systems better at coherently pursuing goals also makes the question of which goals they pursue much more consequential.

r001.rationale: The response discusses losing track of goals and revising ineffective plans, but does not identify memory of past experimental outcomes as a substantial missing capability.

r002.rationale: The response says the issue is not just more memory, but does not state that even a very large context window can be inadequate for tracking the state needed for open-ended goals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing they’re missing is a persistent executive function. They can perform a task when you put it in front of them, but pursuing an open-ended goal means deciding what to work on, breaking that down into subgoals, remembering what you’ve tried, and changing course when something doesn’t work. You need that whole loop to hold together over time.

And some of that might come from scaffolding around a model—memory, tools, feedback—rather than just making the model bigger. But there’s still a question of whether the system can reliably tell when it’s making progress. If it loses track of the objective or can’t recognize its own failures, a longer chain of actions doesn’t necessarily get you closer to the goal.

r001.rationale: The response says systems need to remember what they have tried as part of pursuing open-ended goals, identifying memory of past outcomes as a missing capability.

r002.rationale: The response discusses maintaining the goal loop over time, but does not say that even a very large context window can be inadequate for tracking the needed state.
